description:
Why join us

The idea is simple and flexible, so you’ll have real say in how the game looks and plays.

You’ll get hands-on experience building a complete project from scratch, which is great for your portfolio.

Who we’re looking for

Game developer or programmer (Unity, Godot, Python/Pygame, or web-based)

Artist or UI designer for spacecraft, planets, and menus

Space or science enthusiast to help keep the mission details realistic using NASA data
summary: We developed Mission Architect, an interactive browser-based space mission design and systems engineering simulator built with React, TypeScript, CSS, and HTML5 Canvas. Players guide a spacecraft through four coupled phases—Target Selection, Spacecraft Assembly, Launch & Trajectory, and Live Operations—watching subsystems assemble onto a live CAD blueprint while coupled telemetry meters, a 5-axis trade-off radar chart, and engineering advisories react in real time. Mission Architect addresses the challenge by turning invisible aerospace constraints into tangible cause-and-effect grounded in real planetary physics, including inverse-square solar flux and Deep Space Network attenuation, Δv budgets, radiation belts, and orbital eclipses, so players immediately see how adding an instrument impacts power, data buffers, rocket mass limits, and cost. Animated launch-to-orbit simulations, live anomaly decisions, and NASA-style Mishap Investigation Reports transform failures into clear diagnostic feedback. This is important because students rarely get hands-on experience with end-to-end systems coupling, and making spacecraft architecture playable in any browser builds practical systems-thinking intuition for future space engineers.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Mission Architect is a browser-based space mission design simulator. Players act as NASA mission designers. They choose a destination (the Moon, Mars, the asteroid 16 Psyche or Jupiter’s moon Europa) and a science objective. They then build a spacecraft by selecting power systems, batteries, communications, thermal and radiation protection, a flight computer and science instruments. Finally they choose a launch vehicle and a flight path.

A physics engine recalculates the design after every click. It checks launch mass against the rocket’s limit, power balance in sunlight and eclipse, data generated versus data the antenna can send home, delta-v, thermal conditions, radiation and cost. Live indicators show each result as Nominal, Marginal or Critical, and a radar chart scores five areas. When the design is ready, the player launches the mission. The simulation shows liftoff, the flight to the target, and live graphs of battery, data memory and temperature. Three times during flight, a “live anomaly” such as an X-class solar flare pauses the game and the player must choose a response. The mission ends with a grade from S to F, or a mishap report explaining what failed and how to fix it.

What benefits does it have?

It lets anyone experience real engineering trade-offs without expert tools or prior knowledge. Feedback is instant and in plain language, and failure is safe, so players learn by experimenting. Four ready-made scenarios, from introductory to advanced, give beginners a working starting point.

What is the intended impact?

We want to make space systems engineering understandable and exciting for students, teachers and curious beginners. Players should leave understanding why real missions look the way they do: why Europa needs a nuclear battery, why a Venus flyby needs radiators, and why every extra instrument costs power, mass and money.

What tools, languages and software did you use?

The app is built with React 19 and TypeScript, using Vite for the build system, Tailwind CSS for styling, Motion for animation and Lucide for icons. The spacecraft blueprint and the simulation are drawn on HTML canvas. It runs entirely in the browser with no backend, and no special hardware is needed. The mission data is built from published NASA and space agency figures, such as solar irradiance at each target, signal delays and radiation levels, and from real missions such as NASA’s Psyche.

How is it creative?

It turns mission design into a game. The spacecraft is drawn live as you build it: a nuclear battery bolts onto the hull, and ion propulsion shows a blue plasma exhaust. The player’s choices are tested by realistic crisis events with no single right answer, and a NASA-style mishap report turns failure into learning.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: the numbers and warnings follow real physics and real mission conditions.
  • Accessibility: plain-language advisories, color-coded status and starter scenarios for people with no technical background.
  • Difficulty: four destinations and scenarios that scale from easy (Moon) to hard (Europa).
  • Learning value: instant feedback, failure reports and the chance to retry.
  • Reach: a browser-only app with no installation or API keys.
  • Maintainability: the data, physics engine and interface are separate, so new targets, parts and events are easy to add.
